citations.quote: A regular link diagram is **connected** when its underlying projection graph is connected. It is **alternating** when successive crossing visits along each component switch between overpasses and underpasses. It is **reduced** when no complementary region of the projection sphere has a crossing more than once on its boundary. A connected alternating diagram that is reduced is a **reduced alternating link diagram**.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be an unoriented link type in $S^3$. Its **crossing number** $c(K)$ is the least element of
$$\{\,n\in\mathbb N:\text{some regular diagram of }K\text{ has exactly }n\text{ crossings}\,\}.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Let $P$ be a compact smooth $k$-manifold with boundary, let $N$ be a Hausdorff smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $f:P\times[0,1]\to N$ be jointly smooth with every $f_t$ a smooth embedding. Suppose the family is stationary on neighborhoods of both time endpoints. For every open neighborhood $W$ of its compact track $f(P\times[0,1])$, there is a jointly smooth isotopy $H_t:N\to N$ of diffeomorphisms with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $H_t\circ f_0=f_t$, supported in a fixed compact subset of $W$ and stationary near its time endpoints. No choice axiom is assumed. The empty source and zero-dimensional source are allowed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For Jordan curves $C$ and $C'$ in $\mathbb R^2$,
every homeomorphism $h:C\to C'$ extends to a homeomorphism
$H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ that maps the bounded and unbounded complementary
components of $C$ to the corresponding components of $C'$. In particular each
closed bounded Jordan region is a closed $2$-disk.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: Let $v$ be the repeated crossing and take a short overpassing subarc $a$ through $v$, with endpoints just outside its crossing disk. Each of the four sectors touches exactly one of the two ends of this overpass. Two adjacent sectors cannot belong to the same complementary region: a small transverse crossing of their intervening strand changes the parity of intersection with the finite immersed link cycle on the sphere. This parity is well-defined by filling that cycle modulo two on the sphere, or directly by the signed crossing count of a generic path; a closed path has even intersection with a closed immersed curve, since its individual smoothed Jordan circles each separate the sphere. Thus the repeated sectors are opposite. They touch the two different ends of $a$. Within their common open region join nearby points by a simple smooth arc: a finite chain of coordinate disks along a path gives a polygonal arc, loop erasure makes it simple, and finitely many local roundings smooth it. Extend it to the endpoints of $a$ in their empty small neighborhoods, obtaining an arc $b$ missing the diagram except at its endpoints. It meets $a$ only at those endpoints. Therefore $a\cup b$ bounds a planar bigon disk $J$, with smooth boundary arcs and endpoint corners.

Work in a finite plane chart containing $J$ and the diagram, and use its height realization in three-space. The lifted overpass $\widehat a$ lies above every other strand over its projected points. Choose a height $H$ above the entire compact link. There is a smooth graph disk over $J$ whose boundary over $a$ is exactly $\widehat a$, whose other boundary arc projects to $b$, and whose interior misses the rest of the link. To construct it, set its height to $H$ off a thin inward collar of $a$ and the two endpoint neighborhoods. On that collar interpolate from the prescribed overpass height to $H$, never below the prescribed boundary height. At the unique crossing of $a$ with the remaining diagram there is a positive height gap; a sufficiently thin collar retains it by continuity. Away from that crossing and the endpoint neighborhoods, the projected $a$ has positive separation from the remaining finite diagram, so a thinner collar cannot meet it. In the endpoint neighborhoods the rest of the link is the single continuation of $a$ outside $J$; choose the graph and its end collars there to meet it only at the fixed endpoints. Finite smooth cutoffs give the interpolation. On the remaining boundary $b$ use the high graph height, tapering only within those empty endpoint neighborhoods. This verifies disjointness throughout, even when $J$ contains other projected link strands.

Push the lifted overpass across this actual embedded disk to its other boundary arc. Use [F2] to parametrize the disk as a rounded bigon with its two distinguished boundary arcs; parallel arcs in that parameter disk give the sweep away from the two endpoints. Near an endpoint, both inward boundary directions lie in a cone of angle less than a half-turn, after a small choice of the detour tangent in step 1.1. Choose a coordinate whose derivative is positive on that cone. Truncate the sweeping arcs inside a small endpoint ball and join them to the fixed exterior strand as smooth graphs over this coordinate. Positive graph derivatives and smooth cutoff interpolation give a smooth family of embedded joins, agreeing with the old strand on an outer collar. Thus the whole link, rather than just an arc with unmatched endpoint derivatives, has a smooth embedding isotopy fixed outside the disk neighborhood and these two empty endpoint balls. The disk interior misses the remaining link by step 2.1, and the endpoint balls contain no other strand, so no new collisions occur. Make time stationary and apply [F3]. At the endpoint the replacement projects to $b$, with the endpoint adjustments still inside their empty neighborhoods. Every other crossing and its over-under data are untouched, while $v$ is removed. The endpoint is consequently a regular diagram with exactly $c(D)-1$ crossings of the same smooth link.

If $c(D)=c(L)$, the diagram in step 3.1 would contradict the minimum in [F1]. Hence there is no repeated region at any crossing and $D$ is reduced. The same construction proved the more precise assertion without any minimality assumption. It used no alternation, primeness or connectedness.

Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a nonempty compact smooth embedded surface, possibly disconnected and nonorientable, every component of which has nonempty boundary. The ambient sphere has its standard orientation. The normal-transfer expression $B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ defines a symmetric integral bilinear pairing on the free finite-rank group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, with rational extension. It restricts on each component to its normal-transfer pairing; for cycles $a,b$ on distinct components its value is $2\operatorname{lk}(a,b)$, which need not vanish.

Suppose an embedded product cylinder $W=[-1,1]\times D^2$ meets $F$ exactly in its two end disks, on distinct components. Replace those disks by the lateral annulus and round the seams to obtain $F'$. There is an integral basis in which $B_{F'}$ has matrix $G\oplus[0]$, where $G$ is the entire matrix of $B_F$, including its cross-component entries. Thus its signature is unchanged. The boundary link and its surface collar remain fixed, so $e(F)=-\sum_i\operatorname{lk}(K_i,K_i')$, computed from boundary normal push-offs, is unchanged as well.

A finite sequence of such tubes exists making $F$ connected. All intermediate surfaces still have the original boundary link and collar, no closed components, and finite smooth disk-and-band presentations on their components. The signature and $e$ are preserved throughout.

Assume full AC. Let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth embedded surface with nonempty boundary, possibly nonorientable, with a supplied finite smooth disk-and-band presentation. The ambient three-sphere has its standard orientation. For oriented integral multicurves $a,b\subset\operatorname{int}F$, let $\tau b$ be the cycle consisting of the two small normal pushes over $b$, oriented by projection to $b$. For a one-sided circle this is one circle mapping with degree two, rather than a choice of a single normal direction. Then
$B_F([a],[b])=\operatorname{lk}(a,\tau b)$ defines a well-defined symmetric integral bilinear pairing on $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, independently of representatives and sufficiently small normal pushes. Every integral homology class has an oriented multicurve representative, permitting integer coefficients. The pairing extends to rational homology, with quadratic form $q_F(x)=B_F(x,x)$ satisfying the normal-transfer linking identity.

For an embedded compact subsurface $A\subset F$ with such a finite presentation, the pairing on $A$ is the pullback of $B_F$ under inclusion. If $F$ is oriented and its boundary is one knot, its pairing has matrix $V+V^T$ in any integral basis, where $V$ is the positive-push Seifert matrix. Orientation-preserving ambient isotopies transport the pairing.

For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V;G)\to H_n(U;G)\oplus H_n(V;G)\to H_n(X;G)\xrightarrow{\delta}H_{n-1}(U\cap V;G)\to\cdots$$
is exact, with middle map $(u,v)\mapsto u+v$.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

Let $P$ be a compact smooth $k$-manifold with boundary, let $N$ be a Hausdorff smooth $n$-manifold without boundary, and let $f:P\times[0,1]\to N$ be jointly smooth with every $f_t$ a smooth embedding. Suppose the family is stationary on neighborhoods of both time endpoints. For every open neighborhood $W$ of its compact track $f(P\times[0,1])$, there is a jointly smooth isotopy $H_t:N\to N$ of diffeomorphisms with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$ and $H_t\circ f_0=f_t$, supported in a fixed compact subset of $W$ and stationary near its time endpoints. No choice axiom is assumed. The empty source and zero-dimensional source are allowed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r\subset S^3$ be an
oriented link with $r\ge1$ components and complement $X_L$,
([[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]]), and let
$$\varphi:H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\longrightarrow\mathbb Z$$
be the **total linking homomorphism**, defined as the composite
$$H_1(X_L;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow[\ \sim\ ]{\mathrm{Alex}}\widetilde H^1(L;\mathbb Z)\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^rH^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\xrightarrow{\text{sum}}\mathbb Z,$$
where the first arrow is Alexander duality
([[thm-alexander-duality-for-compact-locally-contractible-subsets-of-a-sphere]]),
each $H^1(K_i;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$ is the orientation-induced
identification, and the last map sums the $r$ coordinates. By
[[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]] the map $\varphi$
may again be written $\pi_1(X_L)\to H_1(X_L)\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathbb Z$; we
denote both composites by $\varphi$ and set $K:=\ker\varphi$.

The **one-variable Alexander module** of $L$ is
$$A_L:=H_1(\widetilde{X_L};\mathbb Z),$$
the first singular homology of the connected infinite cyclic cover
$p:\widetilde{X_L}\to X_L$ classified by $K$
([[thm-classification-of-connected-covering-spaces]],
[[lem-subgroup-quotient-of-universal-cover]],
[[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]), equipped with its
structure of module over $\Lambda=\mathbb Z[t^{\pm1}]$
([[def-the-laurent-polynomial-ring]]) in which $t$ acts by the deck
transformation corresponding to the positive generator of
$\operatorname{Deck}(\widetilde{X_L}/X_L)\cong\mathbb Z$.

**Caveats.** The cover is the one classified by $K=\ker\varphi$; since $K$ is
normal the cover is regular and its deck group is
$\pi_1(X_L)/K\cong\mathbb Z$
([[def-regular-covering]], [[thm-regular-covering-characterizations]], [[cor-deck-group-of-a-regular-covering]],
[[def-deck-transformation-and-deck-group]]). The module $A_L$ is ordinary
integral homology of the cover, with the deck action as its module structure;
no twisting by a representation of the link group is used. The total linking
homomorphism satisfies $\varphi(\mu_i)=1$ for a meridian $\mu_i$ of any one
component, so $r\ge1$ is needed for $\varphi$ to be interesting and $A_L$
depends on the orientations of all components through this map.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For Jordan curves $C$ and $C'$ in $\mathbb R^2$,
every homeomorphism $h:C\to C'$ extends to a homeomorphism
$H:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ that maps the bounded and unbounded complementary
components of $C$ to the corresponding components of $C'$. In particular each
closed bounded Jordan region is a closed $2$-disk.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

derivations.claim: Thicken the two side subsurfaces slightly within $F$ to make an open cover whose overlap retracts to $P$; use their product attaching collars and finite corner charts. The two open sets retract to $A_1,A_2$. Since $H_1(P)=0$ and $H_0(P)\to H_0(A_1)\oplus H_0(A_2)$ is injective, [F2] gives $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)=H_1(A_1;\mathbb Q)\oplus H_1(A_2;\mathbb Q)$. The same cover with the disk $Q$ gives the analogous coordinates for $F^\dagger$, using the same exterior pieces. To identify each old and new side group, cut a cycle at its finitely many passages across $\gamma$ and reconnect its endpoints in the new disk. Two choices of reconnection differ by cycles bounding chains in that disk, so the identification on homology is unambiguous. The identical disk attachment incidences identify the component sets of the old and new side surfaces. The degree-zero sequence also gives $c(F)=c(A_1)+c(A_2)-1=c(F^\dagger)$; the first-Betti-number equality follows from the two direct sums.

Choose finitely many multicurve representatives for bases on the sides. Make their passages across $\gamma$ transverse, avoiding its finite vertices; first-side endpoints then lie in $I_1$ and second-side endpoints in $I_2$. Within $P$ the two families of oriented arcs can be made transverse, and each color is itself embedded. The finitely many choices and perturbations are made in their actual disk and rectangle charts. Cycles on a component not meeting $P$ stay entirely inside its ball. Thus all representative ribbons and transfers miss the corner vertices and depend only on the supplied product collars. The calculation may be made before or after their arbitrarily small compatible roundings, which are smooth isotopies of these ribbons.

The diagonal pairing on either side is unchanged by replacing $P$ first with $Q_0$. For the first side alone, the other ball $Y_2$ contains no part of $A_1$ except its boundary disk. Normalize this ball and window by [F3], so $P,Q_0$ are its upper and lower hemispheres. Write the upper hemisphere as $(\sqrt{1-u^2}\cos\phi,\sqrt{1-u^2}\sin\phi,u)$, $0\le u\le1$. Choose $\chi=1$ near $u=0$ and zero for $u\ge1/2$, and a small $\delta>0$. Sweep it by $r_t(u)=\sqrt{1-u^2-\delta u\chi(u)\sin(\pi t)}$, $z_t(u)=u\cos(\pi t)$, using the points $(r_t\cos\phi,r_t\sin\phi,z_t)$. The radius is strictly decreasing in $u>0$ after choosing $\delta$ small: on the cutoff transition $2u+\delta(\chi+u\chi')\sin(\pi t)>0$, and near zero the added term is nonnegative. The radicand stays positive on that cutoff support. At the fixed boundary $u=0$ the radial and height derivatives never vanish together, and near the pole $\chi=0$, so the original smooth pole coordinates still apply. Its squared norm is $1-u^2\sin^2(\pi t)-\delta u\chi(u)\sin(\pi t)\le1$, strictly less for $u>0$ and $0<t<1$. Thus this is an actual smooth disk sweep through the ball, fixing its edge and joining $P$ to $Q_0$. Retain the first-side exterior ribbons. At an attaching interval the limiting union at $t=1$ has a folded seam, so do not concatenate the raw limiting tangent rays. Stop the sweep just before that time and join its two branches by a short semicircle in each normal product plane. Keep this radius positive while flattening the remaining cap to $Q_0$. Off that semicircle the two branches remain on their distinct ball sides; on it the arc derivative never vanishes. Smooth cutoff interpolation of their positive gaps joins this fold to the unchanged outer ribbons. This is an embedded smooth product-ribbon family, and its endpoint is exactly the stipulated semicircle rounding. All intervals used by these representatives are disjoint and avoid the corner vertices, so their supports can be chosen disjoint. No other first-side ribbon lies inside the sweeping ball. Extend this compact ribbon isotopy by [F3]; the stipulated supported variants of the roundings may be included at the end. Next indent each supplied boundary tab, keeping all attaching windows fixed. Its old and new boundary arcs bound the actual tab disk; [F3] gives a smooth lens parameter with the fixed endpoint collars. Moving one boundary arc across that lens and carrying its inward collar gives an embedding isotopy from the larger disk to the indented disk. The tab interiors and their endpoint collars miss every exterior attaching ribbon, so the finitely many indentations may be made in disjoint supports and introduce no twist. Their endpoint is $Q$. All normal-transfer linking entries within that side therefore agree by [F1]. Use $Y_1$ for the second side. If there is no attaching interval, all side homology representatives miss the disk, whose homology is zero, so this conclusion needs no disk sweep. Denote the unchanged two full diagonal matrices by $G_1,G_2$.

Compute a mixed entry using the orientation of $\Sigma$ as the boundary of $Y_1$. Let $a$ and $b$ be the oriented arcs in $P$ of a first-side and a second-side cycle $c_1,c_2$. Choose the normal-transfer radius of $c_2$ very small. Its portion in $Y_1$ then lies in an arbitrarily thin boundary collar, because $A_2\setminus P$ lies in $\operatorname{int}Y_2$; each arc $b$ has exactly one transferred lift on the $Y_1$ side and one on the $Y_2$ side, both oriented by projection. Push the portions $a$ of $c_1$ into $Y_1$ until the entire pushed cycle lies beyond that thin collar. Outside $P$ this requires only a collar adjustment near its endpoints, away from the disjoint second-side windows. The final cycle has linking zero with the transfer by [F4]. During the push the only crossings of the transfer are its one $Y_1$ lift above each transverse point of $a\cap b$. Removing a small disk from the traced annulus at each crossing shows that the linking change is its signed positive-meridian count. In oriented flat coordinates on $\Sigma$ this sign is one fixed global sign $\eta$ times the oriented intersection of $a$ and $b$; $\eta$ depends only on the chosen side and ambient orientation, not on either cycle. Consequently the old mixed pairing is a fixed sign times their disk intersection count. This argument includes weighted multicurves and gives zero when either cycle misses the disk.

Repeat exactly that calculation on $Q_0$ with the same ball side and ambient orientation, so the fixed sign is unchanged. The common boundary identification reverses disk orientation measured in $\Sigma$: the two disk regions have opposite induced boundary orientations along $\gamma$. Hence reconnection from $P$ to $Q_0$ reverses the intersection number of every two arc families with the same endpoint order. One can also verify this by choosing disk parameters with the same boundary parameter and reflecting one parameter disk; intersection signs reverse pointwise. The tab indentations are orientation-preserving disk embeddings fixing the attachment windows, so they do not alter this arc intersection count when $Q_0$ is replaced by $Q$. Thus every mixed entry changes sign. With the coordinates of step 1.1, the two full matrices are therefore $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}G_1&C\\C^T&G_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}G_1&-C\\-C^T&G_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Their congruence by $\operatorname{diag}(I,-I)$ proves the asserted isometry. All cross-component entries have stayed in their original full diagonal blocks or in this explicitly computed mixed block.

An invertible isometry preserves the kernel, signature and strict sign of the quadratic form, including its zero-dimensional case. The component and rank equalities were proved in step 1.1. Nothing used link primeness, connectedness or orientability of the supplied side surfaces. The assertion concerns the actual supplied marked disk-flip data, including its fold and tab collars.

For the exterior-cap clause set $\Sigma=\widehat U\cup V$, using its supplied compatible smoothing, and parametrize its two ball sides by [F5]. The shadow disk is $P=U$; let $Q_0$ be its complementary disk in $\Sigma$. The actual cap $V$ is a subdisk of $Q_0$. The remaining parts of $\widehat U$ are exactly its supplied boundary tabs, so set $Q=V$. Each piece of the old surface off $U$ lies on one ball side, and its attaching intervals on $\partial U$ are assigned to that side. At an interval there is just one exterior half-sheet, because the original surface is embedded; the finite interval and corner data make these precisely the two disjoint marked families. Thus $A_i=U\cup\overline{(F\setminus U)\cap\operatorname{int}Y_i}$ satisfy the hypotheses. Their components have boundary: an untouched closed component would be a closed component of $F$, while every cut component meets a marked cut edge or the old boundary. Apply steps1.1–5.1 to obtain the full pairing isometry for the two exterior surfaces. Finally the supplied annular collars from their boundary curves back to the boundary link give deformation retractions from the completed spanning surfaces to their exterior portions. Interior representatives and their short normal transfers can be chosen literally in those portions, so [F1] identifies their full pairings, including cross-component entries. This proves the finite-cap consequence from its actual supplied data, with no use of a four-dimensional cap-isotopy observation.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Supply a smooth two-sphere $\Sigma\subset S^3$ with its two parametrized closed ball sides $Y_1,Y_2$, a circle $\gamma\subset\Sigma$ dividing it into closed disks $P,Q_0$, and a closed disk $Q\subset Q_0$, and compact embedded surfaces $A_i\subset Y_i$ satisfying $A_i\cap\Sigma=P$. They may have finitely many compatible smooth corners, and need not be connected or orientable. All their components have nonempty boundary. Along $\gamma$, the portions where $A_1\setminus P$ and $A_2\setminus P$ attach are disjoint unions of finitely many open intervals $I_1,I_2$; their closures may meet at finitely many corner vertices, and gaps with no attachment are allowed. If there is an attaching interval, assume that $Q$ meets $\gamma$ along all the marked windows and is obtained from $Q_0$ by deleting finitely many boundary tabs away from those windows. A boundary tab is a disk bounded by one boundary arc of $Q_0$ and one new arc with the same endpoints; their interiors and the supports of the deletions are disjoint. The case $Q=Q_0$ is included. If there is no attaching interval, $Q$ may instead be any disk in $Q_0$. Supply their actual product attaching collars and compatible corner roundings, with no extra band twists. On the disk-flipped attaching intervals use product semicircle roundings of the folded seams, or supported smooth isotopic variants of those roundings.

Suppose the two sets
$$F=P\cup E_1\cup E_2,\qquad F^\dagger=Q\cup E_1\cup E_2,$$
where $E_i=\overline{A_i\setminus P}$, with those product collars rounded give compact smooth embedded surfaces with nonempty boundary and no closed components. Their boundary links need not be assumed equal. This is a supplied marked spherical disk-flip model, not merely an abstract homeomorphism of surfaces. Then their full rational normal-transfer pairings are isometric, including all cross-component entries. In the direct-sum coordinates obtained by cutting cycles at the attaching intervals and joining them through the disk, the isometry is the identity on the first side and minus the identity on the second. Consequently the component counts, first Betti numbers, signatures and either sign of definiteness are preserved. No primeness assumption is used.

In particular, this conclusion applies to a supplied finite exterior plumbing cap $V$ and shadow $U$ with a completed disk $\widehat U$: assume that $\widehat U\cup V$ has compatible smooth sphere and attaching-collar roundings, meets the exterior surface exactly in the disk $U$, and has the finite boundary-tab pattern just specified. The replacement $(F\setminus U)\cup V$, with its supplied roundings and annular collars back to the boundary link, preserves the full pairing and either definite sign. This last clause requires the actual finite cap data; it does not infer them from a drawing.

Let $D$ be a connected alternating regular link diagram on an oriented projection sphere. Choose either checkerboard color. Put a disk in each region of that color and join the opposite colored sectors at every crossing by a half-twisted band, with the twist chosen so that the boundary follows the over-under diagram. After rounding corners these disks and bands form a compact connected embedded spanning surface $F$ for the represented link. If $D$ has crossings, let $G$ be the corresponding Tait graph and orient its edges arbitrarily. Under the retraction of $F$ onto $G$, write a rational homology class as the unique graph cycle $a=\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e e$. There is a single sign $\epsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ such that
$$q(a)=\epsilon\sum_{e\in E(G)}a_e^2=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau c)$$
for every oriented rational multicurve $c$ representing $a$, where $\tau c$ is its normal transfer. Thus $q$ is positive definite or negative definite on $H_1(F;\mathbb Q)$. For a crossingless connected diagram, use either spanning disk and the zero-dimensional definite form.
For a connected regular link projection on $S^2$ with at least one crossing and either checkerboard coloring, both Tait graphs are connected.

If a connected plane graph has vertex, edge and face sets $V,E,F$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]), then

$$|V|-|E|+|F|=2.$$

Deletion is as in [[def-graph-deletion-contraction-minor-and-subdivision]], the tree boundary case uses [[prop-plane-forest-has-one-face]], and the finite induction is [[thm-induction-principle]].

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.
If a regular link diagram on $S^2$ is connected and alternating, then the represented link is nonsplit.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every connected reduced alternating diagram $D$ of an oriented link $L$ realizes the crossing number of its underlying unoriented link: $c(D)=c(L)$.

Assume full AC. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a nonempty nonsplit oriented smooth link. Suppose $F_+,F_-$ are compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces for $L$, without closed components, whose full rational normal-transfer pairings are respectively positive and negative definite. The surfaces may initially be disconnected or nonorientable. Then both are connected, and $L$ has a connected alternating regular diagram on a smooth projection sphere whose two standard checkerboard surfaces are smoothly ambient isotopic, individually, to $F_+$ and $F_-$, with their boundary orientations transported. The diagram has exactly $b_1(F_+)+b_1(F_-)$ crossings. There is no primeness assumption, and the theorem includes composite nonsplit links. The diagram is not asserted to be reduced.

Assume full AC. If a regular diagram $D$ of a nonempty smooth link $L$ has $c(D)=c(L)$, then no complementary region has any crossing more than once on its boundary. Thus $D$ is reduced, whether or not it is alternating, prime or connected. More precisely, a crossing incident twice to one complementary region can be eliminated by a smooth ambient isotopy of the represented link, yielding a regular diagram with exactly one fewer crossing.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] at each of the actual marked caps and compose its isometries. Induction on the finite sequence gives a full pairing isometry $B_{F_j}\cong B_B$ at every stage, retaining all cross-component terms. Its component-count and rank assertions give $c(F_j)=c(B)=1$ and $b_1(F_j)=b_1(B)$. In particular every $F_j$ is positive definite, including the zero-dimensional case. This argument also covers the empty sequence with the identity isometry.

Put $n=c(D)$. If $n>0$, let $v_B,v_W$ be the numbers of black and white regions. The connected Tait graph of either color has $n$ edges, so its cycle rank is $n-v_B+1$ or $n-v_W+1$: the incidence image is the zero-sum vertex subspace, since connected edge paths generate all differences of vertex vectors. The original projection has $n$ four-valent vertices and $2n$ edges, giving $v_B+v_W=n+2$ by the Euler formula in [F2]. Thus $b_1(B)+b_1(W)=2n-(n+2)+2=n$. For $n=0$ the connected diagram is a circle and its two checkerboards are disks, yielding the same equality. Together with step1.1 this proves $b_1(F_j)+b_1(W)=n$ at every stage.

By [F3] the original smooth link $L$ is nonsplit and $n=c(L)$. Apply [F4] to $F_j$ and the unchanged $W$, which have the required opposite definite pairings by step1.1 and the given labeling. It supplies a connected alternating diagram $D_j$ of the original smooth oriented link and its individual smooth checkerboard classes. Step2.1 makes its crossing count exactly $n$, so $c(D_j)=c(L)$.

Therefore [F5] makes $D_j$ reduced. All surface identifications and orientations are those transported by [F4]; the crossing-minimality comparison adds no geometric move. This holds for every finite stage, with no choice of a prime decomposition or assumption of link primeness. The conclusion does not assert that two such diagrams are flype-related; that remaining technical step requires its own proof.
